extracted.intended_audience: high-school students, coaches, and organizers of mathematical olympiads
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and procedural rules for solving high-school olympiad-style mathematics problems (inequalities, sequences, geometry, combinatorics) together with contest structure and marking procedures for international/national olympiads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-step method for max/min problems
rubrics_metrics.description: A solution of problems concerning finding maximum or minimum values usually involves two steps: (1) get an upper bound or a lower bound of the problem using given conditions and well-known inequalities; (2) show that such an upper bound or lower bound is attainable, and then it is the maximum or minimum value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First derive an appropriate bound (Cauchy, AM-GM, etc.), then construct or exhibit an example achieving the bound to prove optimality. (Mentioned as applicable to the competition's first three problems.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Linearize nonlinear sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: When encountering a problem involving a nonlinear sequence, the first thing to do is to linearize and to simplify the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically, if the sequence expression contains radical terms, try to eliminate these terms to obtain a linear recurrence (often of order 2). Use algebraic manipulation (subtracting shifted relations, etc.) to reduce to linear recurrences and then apply known techniques (characteristic equations, induction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove integrality/divisibility via linearization and induction
rubrics_metrics.description: To show every term of a recursively defined sequence is an integer (or divisible by some integer), transform the nonlinear recursion into a linear relation and use base cases together with induction/monotonicity to deduce integrality and divisibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: subtract shifted recurrence relations to obtain a linear relation like an+2 = 2K an+1 - an, then use initial values to deduce all terms are integers and divisible by 2K as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use labeling/product invariant to determine parity of adjacent-different pairs
rubrics_metrics.description: For an m x n (m>3, n>3) chessboard colored red/blue, label red=1, blue=-1 and consider the product of labels on all adjacent-edge pairs; this product (H) equals 1 when there are even 'good couples' and -1 when odd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify squares into corners, border (excluding corners), and interior. Observe how many times each grid label appears in the product H (2,3,4 times respectively). The parity of the number S of adjacent differently colored neighbor pairs is determined by the product of labels on the border (second part). An alternative solution uses successive color-changing transformations to track parity changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of transformation vs evaluation in parity problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Two standard methods for parity/colouring grid problems: (1) evaluation (use numeric labels/invariants like products or sums to deduce parity); (2) transformation (change a single cell's color and track how the quantity of interest changes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both methods are commonly used; transformations often show how parity changes (e.g., changing one cell on border flips parity iff it has odd number of neighbors), while evaluation finds a global invariant computable from boundary labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic vs synthetic approaches in geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometry problems can be approached either analytically (use coordinates and algebraic manipulation) or synthetically (use classical constructions, projections, similarity, proportional segments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to show a point P is on a fixed line when a metric identity holds, one may set coordinates and derive a linear equation; alternatively construct projections of incenter/circumcenter and use proportionality arguments to get the same result. Choose whichever is simpler or more natural for the given figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma: locus of points in an angle with constant sum of distances to the sides
rubrics_metrics.description: Let angle ∠SAT be given and P move in the angle. If the sum of distances from P to lines AS and AT is constant m, then the locus of P is a segment BC with endpoints on AS and AT satisfying AB = AC = m / sin(alpha). Points inside triangle ABC have strictly smaller sum, points outside have strictly larger sum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this lemma when solving problems that assert 'sum of distances to four side-lines is constant' by decomposing into two such angle-locus conditions and deriving contradictions or structure (e.g., show a quadrilateral must be a parallelogram).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinatorial bound via counting possible blocks
rubrics_metrics.description: For binary sequences over {0,1} with the constraint that every two successive 5-term blocks are different, there are at most 2^5 = 32 distinct 5-term blocks, which imposes an upper bound on the sequence length (≤ 36 in the discussed problem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the pigeonhole principle and enumeration of possible blocks; then try to construct extremal examples meeting the bound to show tightness if possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequality technique: prove per-variable bounds then sum
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove inequalities involving symmetric sums over several variables bounded in an interval, it is natural to prove an inequality for each variable separately and then sum the per-variable inequalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: show 4x^3 + 1 > 3x for each x in [-1, ∞), then add four such inequalities to get a global bound for a,b,c,d. Useful when variables are independent but constrained to the same interval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contest structure and problem/score format (IMO-style)
rubrics_metrics.description: The International Mathematical Olympiad format: 2 days, 3 problems per day, 4.5 hours per day; each problem scored out of 7 (total 42 for an individual). Full team score is 252.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approximately half of participants receive medals; roughly 1/12 get gold; medal counts in approximate ratio gold:silver:bronze = 1:2:3. Special awards may be given for solutions better than the official answer.

rubrics_metrics.name: IMO delegation, problem selection and marking procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Each participating country sends a delegation of a leader, a deputy leader and 6 contestants. Problems are contributed by participating countries and selected by the host country; the host does not provide any problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answer scripts are first marked by each team's leader and deputy leader; the leader presents them to coordinators; the jury (composed of team leaders and a chairman) finalizes problems, sets the marking standard, resolves disputes, ensures translation accuracy, standardizes replies to queries, reconciles marking differences between leaders and coordinators, and sets medal cutoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive contradiction/size-argument technique in combinatorics
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving extremal combinatorial claims (e.g., minimal n so that any subset with a given property must contain a prime), use explicit counterexamples to show lower bounds and size/prime-factor growth arguments to rule out larger sizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example technique: exhibit a set of 15 pairwise coprime composite numbers (squares of primes) to show n>15, then show any set of size 16 with pairwise coprime numbers must contain a prime by comparing smallest prime factors and growth to exceed the universe bound.
